overview: This file concerns Turkish action against Japanese news-agency and newspaper correspondents during World War II. Four telegrams report the expulsions of Eti Moto, the Istanbul correspondent of the Nichi Nichi Shimbun, in November 1942, and Oda, the Istanbul correspondent of the Domei agency, in January 1944. The stated grounds include suspected espionage, photographing military zones, sensational reporting of an impending Turkish coup, abuse of journalistic ethics, and misuse of government facilities. A Department of State transmission memorandum and its enclosed paraphrase show that the information about Eti Moto was circulated to U.S. military, naval, and federal intelligence agencies.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Kelley on expulsion of the Nichi Nichi correspondent
subfiles.from: Robert F. Kelley, U.S. Embassy, Ankara
subfiles.about: Reports that Turkey expelled the Istanbul correspondent of the Nichi Nichi Shimbun to Bulgaria on ten hours' notice.
subfiles.summary: The Turkish Director General of Press told an embassy member that he had expelled the Japanese correspondent of the Nichi Nichi Shimbun from Istanbul to Bulgaria. When asked why, he facetiously said that the correspondent had attempted to surpass even the most sensational American correspondents.

subfiles.title: Telegram from Honaker on Eti Moto's expulsion
subfiles.about: Reports that Eti Moto was expelled from Turkey after suspected espionage and alleged photography in military zones.
subfiles.summary: A reputable source informed Honaker that Eti Moto, identified as a Japanese correspondent of the Nichi Nichi Shimbun, had been expelled from Turkey. Moto had recently been detained on suspicion of espionage, while the alleged immediate offense was taking photographs in military zones. The information was marked confidential and sent as a rush telegram.

subfiles.title: Department of State intelligence transmission concerning Eti Moto
subfiles.to: Military Intelligence Division; Office of Naval Intelligence; Federal Bureau of Investigation
subfiles.about: Transmits the confidential report about Eti Moto to three U.S. intelligence and investigative agencies.
subfiles.summary: The Department of State forwarded information from Istanbul concerning Eti Moto to the Military Intelligence Division, Office of Naval Intelligence, and Federal Bureau of Investigation. The enclosure was described as a paraphrase of strictly confidential telegram no. 313 of November 19, 1942. The routing demonstrates that the correspondent's activities were considered relevant to several branches of U.S. wartime intelligence.

subfiles.title: Paraphrase of Istanbul telegram no. 313
subfiles.about: Paraphrases the confidential telegram reporting Eti Moto's expulsion for alleged military-zone photography.
subfiles.summary: The paraphrase states that Eti Moto, correspondent of the Nichi Nichi Shimbun, had recently been expelled from Turkey for allegedly photographing military zones. It also notes his earlier apprehension on suspicion of espionage. The report came from a confidential, reputable source and was itself classified as confidential.

subfiles.title: Supplementary telegram explaining Eti Moto's expulsion
subfiles.from: Robert F. Kelley, U.S. Embassy, Ankara
subfiles.about: Clarifies that sensational political reporting, rather than espionage suspicions alone, was the immediate cause of the correspondent's expulsion.
subfiles.summary: A Turkish Press Bureau official acknowledged that the Nichi Nichi correspondent was suspected of espionage. The immediate reason for expulsion, however, was reportedly a sensational dispatch describing a grave internal crisis in Turkey. The dispatch predicted an imminent coup d'état that would install a government headed by former Interior Minister Şükrü Kaya.

subfiles.title: Telegram on expulsion of Domei correspondent Oda
subfiles.about: Reports the Turkish Press Bureau's decision to expel Japanese Domei correspondent Oda from Istanbul.
subfiles.summary: The Turkish Press Bureau informed the American representative that it was expelling Oda, the Japanese Domei agency correspondent in Istanbul. The bureau accused Oda of abusing journalistic ethics and misusing facilities granted by the Turkish government. Unlike the 1942 reports, the telegram does not explicitly allege espionage.

interest: The file is useful for studying how neutral Turkey policed foreign correspondents and treated Japanese journalism as a potential wartime security threat. Particularly revealing is the discrepancy among the explanations for Eti Moto's expulsion: espionage, military photography, and a sensational prediction of a coup led by Şükrü Kaya. The State Department's circulation of the report to military intelligence, naval intelligence, and the FBI illustrates how ostensibly journalistic incidents entered the wider U.S. intelligence system. The later Oda telegram also permits comparison between two Turkish expulsions of Japanese correspondents under different stated rationales.
